name: Alpine Skiing
tagline: Racing straight down the fall line, where one hundredth of a second separates legends.
overview: Alpine skiing races a skier down a mountain against the clock. Four disciplines split the job: downhill and super-G are single-run speed events reaching 140 km/h, while giant slalom and slalom demand quick, precise turns through gates set just meters apart. Times are measured to the hundredth, and the combined event adds a speed run to a technical run.

It is the Alps' civic theater: Austria, Switzerland, Italy, and France shut valleys down for race weekends, and tens of thousands line the Hahnenkamm in Kitzbühel each January to watch the Streif. Careers are made on named pieces of snow — the Mausefalle, the Hausbergkante — and a crystal globe counts the way a national title counts in soccer.

Newcomers should know the sport is learned bottom-up: parallel turns before carving, carving before gates. Lessons and rentals cost less than one race ski, and recreational race leagues like NASTAR give any skier a handicap score and a reason to keep improving.
facts: FIS (Fédération Internationale de Ski), founded 1924 in Chamonix
Downhill, super-G, giant slalom, slalom, and alpine combined
Downhill and super-G are one-run speed races; giant slalom and slalom run two heats with times added
The Lauberhorn downhill at Wengen runs 4.4 km with a 1,027 m vertical drop; slalom courses carry 55-75 gates
World Cup downhill racers exceed 140 km/h — Johan Clarey was timed at 161.9 km/h at Wengen in 2013
More than 130 national associations under FIS, with Europe's Alpine nations supplying most World Cup podiums
history: Sondre Norheim tours Norway demonstrating the Telemark and parallel turns — the technical ancestry of every alpine turn.
Hannes Schneider's Arlberg method turns descending into a teachable system and spreads ski schools across the Alps.
The first Alpine World Ski Championships at Mürren give racing its own calendar, separate from Nordic jumping and cross-country.
Alpine skiing joins the Olympics at Garmisch-Partenkirchen with a combined event; Germany's Christl Cranz takes the women's title.
The FIS Alpine World Cup launches from an idea by French journalist Serge Lang — a season-long points race that turns one-off races into a league.
Super-G joins the Olympic program at Calgary, splitting the difference between downhill and giant slalom.
Mikaela Shiffrin passes Ingemar Stenmark's record of 86 World Cup wins, a mark long considered untouchable.
formats: Downhill
The longest, fastest course: full tucks, jumps, and compressions — one run, no second chances.
Super-G
One run at giant-slalom turns on a downhill-length course, typically more than 30 gates at speed.
Giant slalom
Two runs of mid-length carved turns between gates set roughly 10-18 m apart.
Slalom
The tightest test: 55-75 quick gates, cross-blocking, and two runs decided by hundredths.
Alpine combined
One speed run plus one slalom run, times added — the traditional all-rounder's title.
Parallel and team events
Head-to-head bracket racing on mirrored courses, a World Cup and Olympic crowd format.
skills: Carving
Riding the ski's edge so the sidecut, not a skid, steers the turn — the basis of all modern racing.
Link ten clean carved turns on easy terrain; two ski-width rails in the snow are the evidence.
Edging and angulation
Tilting the ski on edge while balancing over it, with angles created at the hip, knee, and ankle rather than the waist.
One-ski drills: lift the inside ski for a whole run, then side-slip on steep pitch to feel edge release and engagement.
Fall line reading
Seeing where gravity pulls straightest and where shape must replace speed.
Ski an entire bowl top to bottom without stopping, then repeat drawing a different line.
Gate technique
Taking the shortest arc: shins and inside hand against the gate while the skis run under it.
Brush-gate sessions at half speed; add tempo only when the line stays tight to the turning pole.
Aerodynamic tuck
The egg position in straights — poles under arms, helmet low, knees together — worth seconds in downhill.
Hold a static tuck on gentle terrain for 30 seconds at a time, then carry it through giant slalom arcs.
Pressure management
Absorbing compressions and terrain like the Streif's Mausefalle while staying weighted over the skis.
Progressive bumps and small jumps; flex ankle, knee, and hip in sequence to swallow the landing.
Start and finish
Explosive poling out of the start gate and a held, high tuck across the finish line.
Twenty timed starts per session; measure reaction and the first three gates, not just the clock.
rules: Four disciplines, two characters: downhill and super-G are one-run speed races; giant slalom and slalom are two-run technical races with combined times deciding.
A gate is passed correctly when both ski tips and both feet cross the imaginary line between the gate's poles — missing one means disqualification.
Racers may slip the course before racing to learn the line, but may not ski through the gates.

Equipment is regulated by FIS: minimum ski lengths per discipline (165 cm slalom, 195 cm giant slalom, 218 cm downhill for men), plus suit thickness and air-permeability limits to cap aerodynamic gain.
Start order draws from world ranking; racers launch at fixed intervals against the clock, not against each other.
Alpine combined adds one downhill or super-G run to one slalom run; the lowest total time wins.
A crash does not end a race — racers who finish count, and those who stop or hike are out.
equipment: One pair per discipline: slalom skis are short and quick, downhill skis long and stable. Race-stock pairs run $800-1,800.
Stiff, precise, and fitted by a bootfitter — the single most important purchase. $400-900.
Slalom poles wear hand and shin guards; downhill poles are bent for the tuck. $100-300 with guards.
FIS-approved helmets are mandatory in racing; slalom adds a chin guard. $150-400.
Skin-tight, padded suit with regulated fabric thickness. $300-900.
Flexible spine armor, standard in junior and speed programs. $100-250.
training: Strength is leg-centric: front squats, split squats, and heavy isometric holds, because a carved turn loads the outside leg with several times body weight.
Energy systems mirror the race: 45-90 second high-lactate efforts plus an aerobic base that survives a six-month season at altitude.
Protect knees and hamstrings with Nordic curls, single-leg Romanian deadlifts, and balance work — ACL injuries are the sport's epidemic.
Summer means glacier camps at Zermatt and Saas-Fee plus dryland conditioning; ski hours never fully stop.
Video review every session — technique lives or dies in single turns, and hundredths hide in posture.
pathway: Ski school
Learn to turn, stop, and ride lifts comfortably — every racer's first hundred days.
Club racing (U8-U16)
Regional clubs introduce gates, skill drills, and age-class races near home.
FIS racing
A FIS license at about 16 opens international starts and national junior championships.
Continental Cup
The Europa Cup or North American Cup — the proving ground below the World Cup.
World Cup and national team
Points, globes, and selection for world championships and the Olympics.
events: FIS Alpine World Cup
The season-long circuit, October to March, awarding crystal globes for overall and per-discipline titles.
Hahnenkamm downhill
Kitzbühel's Streif, every January — the sport's most feared course, watched from the slope by tens of thousands.
Alpine World Ski Championships
Every odd-numbered year since 1931.
Winter Olympics
Alpine events every four years since 1936; five medal events per gender.
Continental Cups
The Europa Cup and North American Cup circuits that feed the World Cup week by week.
legends: Jean-Claude Killy
France — swept all three golds at Grenoble 1968 and retired on top; the sport's first television superstar.
Ingemar Stenmark
Sweden — 86 World Cup wins, almost all in giant slalom and slalom; the greatest technical racer ever measured.
Annemarie Moser-Pröll
Austria — six overall World Cup titles in the 1970s and 62 race wins; downhill's first queen.
Marcel Hirscher
Austria — eight consecutive overall World Cup titles from 2012 to 2019; slalom and giant slalom perfected.
Mikaela Shiffrin
United States — first racer past 100 World Cup wins; the most decorated alpine skier in history.
getting_started: Take lessons on rental gear first — a beginner package costs less than a single race ski.
Learn to stop and turn on blue terrain before dreaming of gates; parallel turns come before carving, carving before racing.
Enter a recreational race league such as NASTAR — a handicap score makes every run measurable.
Spend your first real money on boots fitted by a professional, not on skis.
Add dryland twice a week: cycling for the engine, squats and single-leg work for the turns.
Watch World Cup slalom and follow one racer's hands and hips for a whole run — imitation is the oldest coach.
glossary: The straightest downhill path a ball would roll — the axis every turn is built around.
Setting the ski's metal edge into the snow at an angle to steer or brake.
Creating edge angles with hip, knee, and ankle while keeping the torso balanced and upright.
Turning on the ski's sidecut so the edge cuts, rather than skids, a clean arc in the snow.
The ski's hourglass shape — narrower waist, wider tip and tail — that makes the ski turn when rolled on edge.
Driving the inside hand or shin into a slalom gate to keep the line tight.
The aerodynamic egg position held in straightaways to shed drag.
A straight, fast run down the fall line with no turns.
A skier who tests the course before competitors — no ranking, all risk.
A groomed, marked ski run; racing pistes are closed to the public on race day.

name: Cross-Country Skiing
tagline: Human power over snow, uphill and down — winter's purest engine sport.
overview: Cross-country skiing races athletes over rolling terrain on narrow, lightweight skis, in two distinct techniques: classic, gliding in parallel tracks, and skate, pushing side to side like ice skating. It is winter's purest endurance sport — no lift, no gravity discount, every meter earned by the engine inside the suit.

Norway, Sweden, and Finland treat it as civic religion: Holmenkollen draws tens of thousands up an Oslo hillside, and the Tour de Ski turns the sport into a multi-day stage race with cycling-style drama. Elite skiers post VO2max values above 90 ml/kg/min, numbers matched by almost no other athletes on Earth.

Newcomers should start classic on groomed trails at a Nordic center — rentals, lesson, and trail pass fit inside an afternoon. The first goal is not speed but a quiet kick: planting the ski flat so it grips, then gliding long enough to breathe.
facts: FIS, which has governed Nordic skiing since its founding in 1924
Classic (parallel tracks, diagonal stride and double pole) and skate (free technique) — raced separately
Sprint heats, individual and mass-start distances from 10 to 50 km, skiathlon, and relays
Elite skiers test above 90 ml/kg/min VO2max — among the highest values ever recorded in sport
On the program since the first Winter Olympics, Chamonix 1924; women's events since Oslo 1952
1925 at Johannisbad, now Janské Lázně in the Czech Republic
Centered in Norway, Sweden, Finland, and Russia, with rising programs in Switzerland, the United States, and Japan
history: 7000+ years
Rock carvings at Alta in Norway and ancient wooden ski fragments show skiing as transport long before it was sport.
Two Birkebeiner warriors ski the infant king Håkon Håkonsson to safety — commemorated today by Norway's 54 km Birkebeinerrennet, skied with a 3.5 kg pack.
The first Holmenkollen ski festival near Oslo crowns Nordic champions; cross-country racing gains its cathedral.
Olympic debut at Chamonix 1924; the women's 10 km arrives at Oslo 1952.
The FIS Cross-Country World Cup launches as a season-long circuit of sprints and distance races.
American Bill Koch skates to the front at the world championships; within two seasons FIS separates classic and freestyle events for good.
The first Tour de Ski packs multiple stages and a brutal final climb up the Alpe Cermis into the World Cup calendar.
formats: Sprint and team sprint
A 1.2-1.6 km prologue, then knockout heats of six; the team sprint pairs two skiers over six legs.
Individual start
10, 15, or 50 km against the clock at 30-second intervals — the pure time trial.
Mass start
30 or 50 km side by side, tactics and drafting included; the 50 km at Holmenkollen is the classic's classic.
Skiathlon
Half the race classic, half skate, with a pit-stop ski change in between — 2x7.5 km women, 2x15 km men.
Relay
Four skiers, 4x7.5 km men and 4x5 km women, the first two legs classic and the last two skate.
Ski marathons
Citizens' classics like the 90 km Vasaloppet, run since 1922, fill the trails with fields of thousands.
skills: Diagonal stride
The classic running step: kick one ski flat to grip, glide long on the other, pole in opposition.
Kick-timing drills on a gentle uphill, ten times twenty strides — if the ski slips, the kick came late or light.
Double pole
Both poles plant together; the core crunches and arms compress through the poling motion — the fastest classic move.
Four by four minute double-pole intervals on flat terrain with full compression every stroke.
Skate V2 (one skate)
Pushing to the side with one pole plant per skate, used on fast flats and moderate climbs.
Rhythm drills: twenty V2 strokes per side without breaking cadence; film the hips for rotation.
Skate V1 (offset)
The steep-hill skate with asymmetric poling — one side leads, the other braces.
Eight by 90 seconds on a 6-10 percent grade, switching the lead side at the halfway mark.
Downhill and tuck
Free speed hides on descents: skis parallel, hips over heels, tuck low and still.
Ski every training descent with intent; practice holding a quiet, flexed stance until corners feel boring.
Waxing
Matching kick wax or klister to snow temperature and grain — the classic racer's daily chess game.
Keep a wax logbook; test three candidates at the venue every session and record the snow at noon.
Threshold pacing
Racing the red line for 15-50 km without detonating — the sport's defining skill.
Weekly three by ten minute lactate-threshold intervals at the pace you could hold for one hour.
rules: Free-technique races allow any method, which in practice means skating; classic races forbid it entirely and confine skis to parallel tracks.
Sprint races run a qualification prologue, then knockout heats of six skiers through quarterfinals, semifinals, and a final.
Skiathlon opens classic and finishes skate, with a marked pit where skis are changed — a fumbled exchange can cost a medal.
Relays run 4x7.5 km for men and 4x5 km for women, the first two legs classic and the last two skate.
Fluorinated waxes are banned by FIS as of the 2020-21 season, with equipment tests and sanctions for violations.
Shortcuts, skating in classic zones, or unsporting blocking bring disqualification from the jury.
equipment: With a grip zone underfoot for wax or built-in skins; a first pair runs $150-400, race models $600-900.
Shorter, stiffer, no grip zone. $250-500 entry, $700-1,000 race stock.
NNN and SNS systems dominate; boots are flex-rated for each technique. Boots $150-500.
Carbon, sized to the shoulder for classic and the chin for skate. $100-400.
Kick waxes, klisters, cork, scraper, iron, and glide wax — $60-300 to start.
Summer training on pavement with rubber ferrules for grip. $200-450.
training: Volume builds champions: professionals log 700-900 hours a year, mostly low intensity — amateurs should target 300 with patience.
Two hard sessions weekly: VO2max intervals of four by four minutes and lactate threshold of three by ten minutes, on snow or rollerskis.
Rollerski and run with poles in summer; sport-specific load keeps technique and spares the knees from running-only attrition.
Strength double-poles the body: dips, pull-ups, heavy rows, and anti-rotation core work feed the poling engine.
Train both techniques weekly — modern race programs mix styles, and skiathlon demands both in one morning.
pathway: Nordic center and school programs
Groomed trails, rental fleets, and after-school ski clubs — the sport's front door in snowy regions.
Junior club racing
Regional youth series and junior nationals; talent identification happens here, usually between ages 10 and 16.
National junior and college ranks
Junior World Championships at U20 and U23, or NCAA skiing in the United States.
Continental circuit
Scandinavian Cup and similar series — the bridge to full World Cup starts.
World Cup and national team
Season-long circuit, Tour de Ski, world championships, and the Olympics.
events: FIS Cross-Country World Cup
The annual league of sprints and distance races, November to March, with crystal globes for overall, distance, and sprint.
Tour de Ski
A multi-day stage race each New Year, finishing up the Alpe Cermis wall in Val di Fiemme.
Nordic World Ski Championships
Every odd-numbered year, shared with ski jumping and nordic combined.
Winter Olympics
Cross-country has been on the program since Chamonix 1924.
Vasaloppet
The 90 km classic from Sälen to Mora, Sweden, since 1922, with a field of roughly 15,800 skiers.
Holmenkollen Ski Festival
Oslo's March institution — 50 km finals in front of a hillside crowd.
legends: Bjørn Dæhlie
Norway — eight Olympic golds and six overall World Cup titles in the 1990s; the benchmark all endurance skiers are measured against.
Marit Bjørgen
Norway — fifteen Olympic medals, the most of any Winter Olympian, spanning sprints and 50 km finals.
Therese Johaug
Norway — the dominant distance skier of the 2020s, with three golds at Beijing 2022.
Sixten Jernberg
Sweden — nine Olympic medals across the 1950s and 1960s; the first superstar of the long races.
Bill Koch
United States — 1976 Olympic silver and the 1982 overall World Cup title; the skater who changed how the sport moves.
getting_started: Start at a Nordic center with a rental package and one lesson — about $40-70 covers trail pass, skis, and coaching for a morning.
Master the kick before the glide: a balanced diagonal stride beats a hundred frantic pole plants.
Size poles to the chin for skate, the shoulder for classic — wrong length ruins both techniques.
Buy boots first, then poles; skis can be rented until you know which technique you prefer.
Run or cycle in the off-season and try rollerskis — the engine is transferable, the snow is not required.
Enter a citizens' loppet — nearly every snowy town hosts a 10-25 km race with a start wave for every pace.
glossary: Racing in parallel tracks with diagonal stride and double pole — the original style.
Pushing skis outward in a V like ice skating — legal only in free-technique races.
The classic running step, one kick and one glide at a time.
Both poles planting together to compress the core and accelerate the skis.
The wax pocket under the foot of a classic ski that grips when weighted.
Sticky gel wax for coarse or transforming snow — legendary grip, legendary mess.
A classic ski with a mohair strip built into the kick zone — grip without waxing.
A race split half classic, half skate, with a pit-stop ski change between.
A citizens' mass-participation ski race — the sport's community heart.
Running out of glycogen mid-race; prevention is pacing, feeding, and training.

name: Freestyle Skiing
tagline: Moguls, aerials, halfpipe, and big air — gymnastics with skis, judged to the tenth.
overview: Freestyle skiing is judged skiing: athletes perform runs or tricks that panels score for difficulty, execution, and style. Six Olympic disciplines share the tent — moguls, aerials, halfpipe, slopestyle, big air, and the racing offshoot ski cross — each with its own course, judging scale, and subculture.

The sport grew from 1960s American hot dogging into a global progression machine, with the X Games as its laboratory and the Olympics as its crown. Trampoline-first training means twelve-year-olds learn triple flips before they drive, and stars like Eileen Gu turn finals into mainstream television.

Newcomers should know the progression ladder: trampoline, water ramp, airbag, then snow. Air sense is trainable, fear is managed with repetition, and a mogul field is still the best teacher of balance the mountains offer.
facts: FIS runs the Olympic disciplines and World Cup; rider-led events like the X Games shape style and progression
Moguls, aerials, halfpipe, slopestyle, big air, and ski cross
Moguls since 1992, aerials since 1994, ski cross 2010, halfpipe and slopestyle 2014, big air 2022
Moguls score turns 60 percent, air 20 percent, speed 20 percent; halfpipe and slopestyle runs are judged to 100 points
Mogul courses run 235-270 m with two jump lines; aerial landings sit on a hill steepened to about 37 degrees
Olympic superpipes stand 6.7 m (22 ft) from floor to lip
history: Hot doggers flip and spread-eagle down California and Vermont slopes; mogul competitions and early aerial shows organize into a scene.
FIS recognizes freestyle and imposes equipment and safety rules — competitive hot dogging becomes a regulated sport.
The first FIS Freestyle World Ski Championships at Tignes, France.
Moguls debuts at Albertville with France's Edgar Grospiron winning the first gold; aerials follows at Lillehammer 1994.
The first Winter X Games anoint halfpipe and big-air culture as mainstream spectacle.
Slopestyle and halfpipe join the Olympics at Sochi; Eileen Gu's two golds and a silver at Beijing 2022 seal the superstar era.
formats: Moguls and dual moguls
A steep bumped course with two jumps; duals run head-to-head on parallel lines.
Aerials
Flips and twists off a kicker onto a 37-degree landing hill, scored by form times degree of difficulty.
Halfpipe
A 6.7 m superpipe; amplitude, rotation, grabs, and flow judged out of 100.
Slopestyle
One run chaining rails, boxes, and jumps into a single judged descent.
Big air
One enormous jump, three attempts, best two scored — the purest trick contest.
Ski cross
Four skiers race a course of rollers, banks, and gaps at once — freestyle's only pure race.
skills: Mogul absorption
Flexing the legs to swallow each bump while the torso stays quiet — speed survives only through quiet upper bodies.
Ten runs on a gentle mogul field focused only on still hands and head; add speed only when the line stays straight.
Air sense
Knowing which way you are spinning mid-air and what the ground is doing — the skill under every trick.
Trampoline work three times weekly: straight bounces, then half and full twists, 200 touches a session.
Takeoff and landing
Even pops off the lip, knees up in the air, hips under the feet on landing.
Water-ramp and airbag progressions: straight airs, then layouts, then twists — twenty clean landings before each step.
Grabs
Hands on the skis mid-rotation — mute, tail, Japan — the style points that separate clean runs from rotations alone.
Grab every jump from the smallest onward; hold each grab a full second before releasing.
Spins
Rotations from 360 to 1440, frontside and backside, on-axis and corked.
Count rotations on the trampoline; take each new increment to the airbag before the mountain.
Rail riding
Sliding boxes and rails balanced over the skis — commitment and low speed to start.
Flat boxes first, one rail session weekly all winter, eyes at the end of the feature.
Run composition
Building a scored run: amplitude, variety, difficulty, and landings arranged to maximize the rubric.
Study judging sheets with a coach; design and film mock runs, then rebuild them from the scores.
rules: Moguls are scored out of 100: turns 60 percent from a five-judge panel, aerial maneuvers 20 percent from two judges, speed 20 percent against a pace time.
Aerials multiply a form score by each jump's degree of difficulty, so a harder trick done worse can lose to a simple one done perfectly.
Halfpipe, slopestyle, and big air runs are judged to 100 points for difficulty, amplitude, variety, execution, and progression.
Big air counts an athlete's best two of three jumps, rewarding consistency alongside difficulty.
Helmets are mandatory in all FIS freestyle competition; landing zones are stepped, netted, and padded.
Dual moguls run head-to-head on parallel courses; the higher-scoring skier advances through a bracket.
equipment: Upturned tails for switch landings — the park and pipe workhorse. $400-900.
Shorter and softly flexing for absorption. $400-800.
Softer flex than alpine racing for control on landings and rails. $300-700.
Mandatory in competition; full coverage saves more careers than it costs. $100-300.
Padded shorts and hip protection for rail weeks and hard learning days. $40-120.
The off-season classroom — a home trampoline is the sport's best value purchase. $300-800.
training: Trampoline before everything: three sessions a week builds rotation sense that transfers directly to snow.
Summer camps move tricks from trampoline to water ramp to airbag; land twenty clean repetitions before taking anything to a real landing hill.
Power over endurance: single-leg squats, hip hinges, and plyometrics for landings that load five or more times body weight.
Ski moguls weekly regardless of discipline — bumps teach absorption that jumps never will.
Visualize full runs daily; judged sports are won in rehearsal as much as repetition.
pathway: Resort park programs
Intro park camps and small features — the entry for most kids between 6 and 12.
Club and academy teams
Mogul pipelines or park-and-pipe squads with trampoline, water ramps, and coach-led progression.
Regional series
NorAm, Europa Cup, and Revolution Tour events — first FIS points and rankings.
World Cup
Annual circuits per discipline, from the season opener in Ruka to the March finals.
X Games and Olympics
Invitation and qualification via rankings; the top of a very public pyramid.
events: Winter Olympics
Six freestyle disciplines on the program since Beijing 2022.
FIS Freestyle Ski World Championships
Every odd-numbered year across all disciplines.
FIS World Cup
Annual per-discipline circuits; moguls open each season at Ruka, Finland.
X Games
Aspen each January since 1997 — the culture's proving ground for new tricks.
FIS Junior World Championships
The U20 pipeline for aerialists and mogul skiers.
legends: Alexandre Bilodeau
Canada — first Canadian to win Olympic gold on home soil (moguls, Vancouver 2010), then defended it at Sochi 2014.
Mikael Kingsbury
Canada — the most decorated mogul skier ever, with PyeongChang 2018 gold and a record shelf of World Cup wins.
Eileen Gu
China — born in the United States, competing for China; two golds and a silver at Beijing 2022 at age 18.
Sarah Burke
Canada — four-time X Games halfpipe champion whose campaigning put superpipe skiing on the Olympic program; died training in 2012.
Jonny Moseley
United States — 1998 Olympic moguls gold landed with a 360 mute grab; freestyle's showman.
getting_started: Start in a beginner park: mini jumps and flat boxes at low speed, one feature at a time.
Book trampoline sessions — most ski academies run them year-round and they are the fastest route to air sense.
Ski moguls every week; absorption learned there shows up in every landing you will ever make.
Wear a helmet always, and impact shorts through the rail-learning phase.
Film every trick and review it the same day — progression in judged sports is video-driven now.
Find a club or academy program once the jumps outgrow the lesson format; coaching is the difference between progression and injury.
glossary: A course of snow bumps skied with rhythm, two jumps, and judged turns.
Flips and twists off a kicker onto a steep landing hill, scored by form and difficulty.
A U-shaped snow channel; height, rotation, and grabs are judged on each wall.
A judged run through rails and jumps combining the park's whole vocabulary.
One giant jump, best two of three scored — trick-taking at maximum size.
An off-axis rotation where the head drops below the hips mid-spin.
An off-axis flip-rotation hybrid, tumbling backward through the spin.
Holding a ski mid-air — the style marker judges reward.
Sliding or playing on any feature: rails, boxes, walls, bonnets.
Landing a trick cleanly, directly on the feet — the word every edit wants.

name: Ski Jumping
tagline: Two hundred meters of human flight — aerodynamics, courage, and style points over Planica.
overview: Ski jumping sends athletes down an inrun at up to 100 km/h, off a takeoff table, and into a flight of 100 to 250 meters, scored for distance and style. The landing is a telemark — one leg forward, deep bend — and five judges grade the whole sequence from takeoff to outrun.

Norway invented it; Poland, Austria, and Germany worship it. The Four-Hills Tournament packs stadiums through the New Year, and Planica's flying hill is a March pilgrimage. No sport merges physics and nerve so nakedly — a jump is a wind tunnel reading made human.

Newcomers should know that everything is measured: ski length is capped at 145 percent of body height, inrun gates adjust for weight and wind, and juniors start on 10-to-30-meter hills inside clubs that lend the gear. Courage matters; geometry matters more.
facts: FIS, which has governed ski jumping since its 1924 founding
Normal hills HS106-109, large hills HS134-140, ski flying hills HS200-240
Jumps of 90-140 m on Olympic hills; flying-hill records have passed 250 m at Vikersund and Planica
Distance points plus style points from five judges, with wind and gate compensation equalizing conditions
Men's events since Chamonix 1924; women's since Sochi 2014; mixed team since Beijing 2022
Ski length capped at 145 percent of body height, with weight-based adjustments to inrun gates
Inside the FIS Nordic championships since 1925; dedicated ski-flying world titles since 1972
history: Danish-Norwegian officer Olaf Rye launches himself 9.5 m as a military demonstration — the first recorded ski jump.
Organized competitions spread from Trysil and Morgedal; the first Holmenkollen festival in 1892 makes jumping Norway's winter showpiece.
Josef Bradl becomes the first jumper past 100 m, at Planica.
The Four-Hills Tournament begins its German-Austrian tour of Oberstdorf, Garmisch-Partenkirchen, Innsbruck, and Bischofshofen — jumping's annual Super Bowl.
Sweden's Jan Boklöv popularizes the aerodynamic V-style, worth meters over the old parallel position, and it soon becomes universal.
Finland's Toni Nieminen breaks the 200 m barrier at Planica.
Women jump at the Olympics for the first time at Sochi, a decade after the first women's World Cup season of 2011-12.
formats: Normal hill individual
Two competition rounds from the HS106-109 hill, cut to the top 50 after round one.
Large hill individual
The same format on HS134-140, where distances push past 140 m and flight time stretches beyond four seconds.
Team events
Four jumpers per nation over two rounds; men's and mixed-team titles at the Olympics.
Ski flying
On HS200-240 hills only, with flatter takeoffs, longer flights, and its own world championships since 1972.
Summer jumping
Plastic and ceramic inruns keep the circuit alive June through October, with a summer Grand Prix.
skills: Inrun crouch
A still, aerodynamic crouch on the bars — any wobble in the last meters costs distance.
Video every inrun; dryland holds of a 60-second static crouch build the stillness.
Takeoff timing
The single explosive extension off the table, timed to the final meter — the most-trained movement in the sport.
Box jumps onto mats simulate the table; fifty coached repetitions per session, rhythm counted aloud.
Flight position
Body stretched flat over skis held in a V, arms locked — the shape that turns height into glide.
Wind-tunnel camps for national teams; at club level, glide drills on small hills and constant video.
Telemark landing
One leg forward, deep bend, arms quiet — style points and knee protection in one motion.
Landing reps from small hills, scored 0-20 exactly as judges would; the outrun must follow calm.
Wind reading
Headwind lifts, tailwind drops; the flags, the anemometers, and the gate board tell the story before the bar opens.
Study live gate changes on broadcasts; keep a notebook pairing readings with distances.
Weight management
Weight sits inside the equipment rules: dropping below the norm shrinks your skis and your inrun gate.
Team nutritionists set targets; strength work preserves lean mass and health inside the limits.
Composure
The bar drops onto a 100-meter drop with 30,000 watching; adrenaline must become stillness.
Breathing routines and full-run visualization before every single jump, training included.
rules: Score is distance plus style: the K-point is worth 60 points, each meter beyond adds 2.0 points on normal hills and 1.8 on large hills, with subtraction for short jumps.
Five style judges mark takeoff, flight, and landing out of 20 each; the highest and lowest marks are dropped.
Wind and start-gate compensation add or subtract points, so a headwind jump is not punished and a tailwind jump is not gifted.
Suits must pass strict permeability and size checks — fabric that catches air is banned because it can both add meters and kill.
Ski length follows a 145 percent body-height cap with BMI-based adjustments, a rule designed to end dangerous weight loss.
A jump counts only if the landing is ridden to the outrun; falls bring heavy style deductions and can void the result.
equipment: Wide, long, and regulated — 145 percent of body height at most. $600-1,200.
A snug, permeability-tested one-piece that must pass FIS checks. $300-700.
Low-profile, tuned for inrun glare and landing light. $50-150.
Rear-flexing jumping boots that let the ankle load the takeoff. $200-500.
Special low-friction waxes matched to snow and temperature — teams guard their formulas.
training: Dryland is the year's bulk: trampoline, imitated jumps onto mats, sprints, and mobility — snow time is precious and rationed.
Explosive power for one second of takeoff: hurdle hops, box jumps, and jump squats.
General strength and core hold the flight shape; flexibility protects hips and hamstrings in the flat position.
Hill progression is coach-gated: K10 to K40 for juniors, plastic hills in summer, big hills only on clearance.
Mental training is formal: visualization, routines, and debriefs after every session — courage is organized here.
pathway: Club small hills
Children start at 6-9 on K10-K30 plastic or snow hills; clubs lend skis and suits.

Age-class competitions and national junior championships through the teens.

Expect to borrow first: clubs lend starter skis, suits, and helmets; the barrier is courage, not cash.
Take trampoline classes — takeoff timing transfers directly from mat to table.
Follow the coach-gated progression through hill sizes; nobody jumps a bigger hill uninvited.
Watch Four-Hills broadcasts with the inrun camera on — it teaches flight position better than any diagram.
Build a gymnast's profile: legs, core, and mobility transfer better than size.
glossary: The ramped start chute where jumpers accelerate to 90-100 km/h before the table.
The curved lip at the inrun's end — the launch point where the jump begins.
The hill's calibration point, worth 60 points; distance is measured from it.
The official size measure of a jumping hill, from HS106 normal hills to HS240 flying hills.

The flat run-out after landing where the jump slows to a stop.
Skis held in a V during flight, the aerodynamic standard since the late 1980s.
Competition on HS200-plus hills, a discipline of its own since 1972.
The adjustable bar on the inrun — higher gates mean more speed, and the jury sets it for safety.
Points added or subtracted for headwind and tailwind so jumps stay comparable.

name: Nordic Combined
tagline: Jump in the morning, race 10 kilometers in the afternoon — winter's two-event test.
overview: Nordic combined asks one athlete to be two specialists: a ski jumper and a cross-country racer. The jumping result sets the start order — the Gundersen method converts jump points into seconds — and the 10 km race that follows is a literal chase, first across the line wins.

Norwegians call it kongsgrenen, the king's discipline, and it headlined the first Winter Olympics in 1924. Its drama is built in: a perfect jump buys a head start, one wobble hands the peloton a weapon, and the finish is the most legible in Nordic sport.

Newcomers should know both parents matter: kids who run and jump early adapt best, and clubs that offer hill and track together are the entry point. The women's World Cup, running since 2020, is still fighting for the Olympic place the men's program has held for a century.
facts: Ski jumping points convert to start seconds — one point equals four seconds in the individual Gundersen format
One competition jump from the normal or large hill, then a 10 km cross-country pursuit
FIS — nordic combined has sat under the federation since its 1924 founding
On the program since Chamonix 1924; team events since 1988; no women's Olympic events yet
The sport demands both jump power and a 90-plus VO2max — a rare physiological double
1925 at Johannisbad, part of the Nordic world championships ever since
Strongest in Norway, Germany, Austria, Finland, Japan, and France
history: Norwegian village meets and military drills jump and race on the same day — the combination is the original test of a complete skier.
The first Holmenkollen festival crowns a combined champion three decades before the Winter Olympics exist.
Nordic combined headlines the first Winter Olympics at Chamonix.
Gunder Gundersen's pursuit format — jumping points as start seconds — is adopted at the world championships and then the Calgary Olympics, replacing point totals with a visible chase.
Germany's Eric Frenzel and Johannes Rydzek lead a golden generation as the compact one-jump-plus-10-km format becomes standard.
The first women's World Cup season launches at Ramsau in December 2020 — the long road to Olympic inclusion begins in earnest.
formats: Individual Gundersen
One jump, then 10 km of skating cross-country from converted start times — the World Cup staple.
Two-jump individual
Two jumps from the hill and 10 km of racing, used at some world championships.
Mass start
A 10 km mass-start race first, jumping afterward; results convert to points.
Team relay (4x5 km)
Four jumpers whose points set one team start, then four 5 km legs at the Olympics and championships.
Team sprint
Two athletes pool their jump points and split the cross-country legs.
skills: Takeoff timing
The same explosive table jump the specialists train — one second that buys or costs 20 meters.
Mat-jump drills from boxes, fifty repetitions per session with a coach counting the rhythm.
Glide composure
Holding the aerodynamic V while the ground falls away — a jumper's panic lives in the first second of flight.
Summer plastic-hill volume: hundreds of small jumps build the glide reflex one meter at a time.
Skate technique
The cross-country leg is skated at full racing speed, on the same gear the distance specialists use.
Rollerski intervals twice weekly; four by four minute VO2max pieces on rolling terrain.
The transition
From outrun to race start in about an hour: helmet off, legs switched on, adrenaline repurposed.
Train the switch deliberately — jump in the morning, race a hard 3 km piece an hour later, weekly.
Chase pacing
Starting 30-90 seconds back means racing a clock you cannot see, alone at the front of your own race.
Time-trial 10 km pieces against split targets; learn your exact per-kilometer threshold pace.
Downhill courage
Descents at 60 km/h on thin skis, minutes after 100 meters of flight — composure must be rationed.
Ski every training descent aggressively; practice tucks immediately after hard climbs.
Nerves under deficit
A bad jump hands you a chase that feels hopeless; the sport rewards those who race it anyway.
Set process goals like split times instead of place goals; rehearse comeback races in training series.
rules: Jump points convert to start seconds at one point equals four seconds in individual Gundersen racing.
The track decides everything after the start: the first racer across the 10 km finish line wins, with no post-race points arithmetic.
Jumping is judged as in ski jumping — distance from the K-point plus five style judges, high and low marks dropped.
The cross-country leg uses free skate technique, usually over two 5 km laps of a closed course.
In the Olympic team event, four athletes' jump points merge into one team start for a 4x5 km relay.
Athletes carry two full setups: jumping skis governed by the 145 percent rule on the hill, skating skis on the track — service crews wax both.
equipment: Regulated to 145 percent of body height, tuned per hill. $600-1,200.
Race-grade skating pairs, waxed for glide. $400-900.
Boots $250-500, carbon poles sized to the chin $150-400.
A skating skinsuit for the track, plus warmups for the outrun-to-start window. $150-400.
training: Split days build both engines: jump or imitate in the morning, endurance in the afternoon — the classic combined double.
Endurance volume of 500-600 hours a year with weekly threshold and VO2max blocks.
Explosive strength for the takeoff: hurdle hops, box jumps, heavy squats — power, not size.
Summer plastic-hill camps and winter hill sessions keep jumping volume alive without snow dependence.
Recovery is part of the job: two technical sports means sleep, food, and load management are coached, not optional.
pathway: Club juniors
Kids learn cross-country and small-hill jumping together from about age 8 — the sport's ideal entry.
National junior ranks
Junior championships and Junior World Championships through the teens.

The international development circuit below the World Cup.

The annual circuit of Gundersen races across the Nordic heartlands.

Rollerski in summer, jump on mats year-round; the sport is built on repetition of two very different rhythms.

Norwegian for the king's discipline — the sport's nickname at home.

The required one-leg-forward landing on the hill.
The free-technique skating style used for the cross-country leg.
Both poles planting together — the combined racer's flat-terrain weapon.

A summer jumping hill with brushed plastic or ceramic inrun surface for year-round jumping.

name: Snowboarding
tagline: One board, four edges, and a halfpipe wall taller than a two-story house.
overview: Snowboarding rides a single board with a sideways stance: halfpipe, slopestyle, and big air are judged for amplitude, difficulty, and style, while snowboard cross and parallel giant slalom race head to head. Every discipline begins from the same two tools — heel edge, toe edge — and one stance choice: regular or goofy.

The sport began as a toy and a rebellion — Sherman Poppen's 1965 Snurfer, Jake Burton Carpenter's Vermont garage — and reached the Olympics at Nagano in 1998. It changed winter sports culture permanently: baggy pants became committee rooms, video parts became resumes, and style became a scoring criterion rather than a bonus.

Newcomers should take one lesson and expect sore wrists: heel side, toe side, linked turns, then tiny park features. Regular or goofy is decided by which foot you lead with sliding across a smooth floor — and the wrong guess only costs a binding swap.
facts: FIS runs Olympic qualification and the World Cup; the X Games and rider-led events shape culture and progression
Halfpipe, slopestyle, big air, snowboard cross, parallel giant slalom, and parallel slalom
Debuted at Nagano 1998; big air added at PyeongChang 2018
Olympic superpipes stand 6.7 m (22 ft) from floor to lip
Regular means left foot forward, goofy means right — the rider's first choice before any binding is mounted
The FIS Snowboard World Championships date to 1996
World Cup stops across North America, Europe, and Asia, with Japan and China now major medal powers
history: Sherman Poppen bolts two skis into the Snurfer for his daughters in Muskegon, Michigan — the toy that starts everything.
Jake Burton Carpenter founds Burton Snowboards in Vermont; Tom Sims and others turn backyard prototypes into an industry.
Ski areas lift their bans one by one as national races and magazines build a scene from underground to mainstage.
Snowboarding debuts at the Nagano Olympics; Canada's Ross Rebagliati wins the first gold, in giant slalom.
Halfpipe becomes the marquee through Shaun White's era, and slopestyle joins the Olympics at Sochi 2014.
Big air enters at PyeongChang; Ayumu Hirano's triple cork 1440 and Chloe Kim's back-to-back titles reset the ceiling at Beijing 2022.
formats: Halfpipe
A judged run wall to wall in a 6.7 m superpipe — amplitude, rotation, grabs, flow.
Slopestyle
Rails, boxes, and jumps chained into one judged descent.
Big air
One massive kicker, three jumps, best two scored.
Snowboard cross
Four to six riders race a course of rollers, berms, and features — contact included.
Parallel giant slalom
Head-to-head bracket racing on mirrored courses, decided by combined times.
skills: Edge control
Pressure and release on heel and toe edges — every turn, check, and landing starts here.
Garland drills: ride one edge across the hill and release to flat, twenty repetitions per edge.
Ollie and nollie
Popping off the tail or nose without a lip — the foundation of all park riding.
Ten ollies on every flat run; measure progress against your own bindings.
Spins
180 through 1080 and beyond, frontside and backside, switch included.
Trampoline and airbag progressions; land each rotation ten times clean before sizing up.
Grabs
Method, melon, indy, stalefish — hands decide style scores as much as rotation does.
Grab every jump from day one and hold each grab a full second before release.
Pipe riding
Reading the transition and pumping walls for amplitude — speed is generated, not just carried.
Progress pipe sizes in order: 8-foot walls long before 22-foot superpipes; take a pipe-specific lesson early.
Jibbing
Boardslides and 50-50s on rails and boxes, balanced and unbothered.
Flat boxes first at walking speed; eyes at the end of the feature, always.
Boardercross tactics
Pack racing over rollers and berms — line choice, drafting, and passing under contact.
Race friends on a natural course; practice following tight for three features, then swinging outside to pass.
rules: Judged events — halfpipe, slopestyle, big air — score runs to 100 points for difficulty, variety, amplitude, execution, and progression.
Big air counts an athlete's best two of three jumps; consistency with difficulty wins, one-hit runs do not.
Snowboard cross runs four to six riders at once; racing contact is part of the sport, deliberate interference is a disqualification.
Parallel giant slalom races two riders on mirrored courses; the faster combined time advances the bracket.
Helmets are mandatory in FIS competition, and course inspection happens at low speed only, before racing.
Halfpipe and slopestyle finals usually trim the field — qualification decides who rides the last runs.
equipment: All-mountain decks $300-600; park boards with durable bases and edges $250-500.

training: Skateboard and surf in the off-season — edge control and fear calibration transfer almost one-to-one.
Trampoline for spins, slackline for balance — the judged disciplines are won in the summer.
Strength for landings: unilateral leg work, hip hinges, and rotational core for spins and checks.
Interval conditioning matches pipe runs: 45-90 second all-out efforts, repeated with recovery.
Ride in good conditions — early-morning corduroy for carving, softened landings for new tricks; frustration and injury live in bad snow.

name: Biathlon
tagline: Ski hard, then shoot straight — a race where one heartbeat costs a medal.
overview: Biathlon alternates maximum-effort cross-country skiing with rifle marksmanship: race a loop, stop at the range, hit five targets from prone or standing, then race again. Every miss costs a 150 m penalty loop or, in individual races, a full minute — the sport's cruel arithmetic.

Born from Scandinavian military patrol skiing, it is now winter's television giant in Germany, Norway, and France, drawing six-figure on-site crowds at Oberhof and Antholz. The appeal is legible: the world's fittest skiers trying to hold a rifle still while their pulse exceeds 170.

Newcomers should know the range is where races are won and lost, that prone targets are 45 mm wide and standing targets 115 mm, and that the rifle rides the back the whole race. Start with a club that uses laser or air rifles — the ski fitness, not the gun, is the long project.
facts: Ski as fast as possible, then slow the pulse enough to hit 45 mm (prone) or 115 mm (standing) targets at 50 m
IBU — International Biathlon Union, founded 1993 from the old pentathlon federation
Sprint, pursuit, individual, mass start, relays, and mixed relays
A miss means a 150 m penalty loop, about 20-25 seconds, or a one-minute penalty in individual races
Smallbore .22 long rifle, minimum 3.5 kg with harness, carried on the back throughout
Men's biathlon since Squaw Valley 1960; women's since Albertville 1992
history: Norwegian-Swedish border patrols hold the first recorded ski-and-shoot contest — the sport grows straight out of soldiering.
Military patrol, biathlon's ancestor, is a medal event at the first Winter Olympics in Chamonix.
The first modern World Championships at Saalfelden formalize the 20 km individual as the sport's core test.
Biathlon joins the Olympic program at Squaw Valley, with the 20 km individual as the only race.
The IBU is founded and rebuilds the sport for television — pursuits, mass starts, and relays turn penalties into visible drama.
Ole Einar Bjørndalen collects eight Olympic golds; Martin Fourcade answers with five and seven straight overall World Cup titles.
formats: Sprint
7.5 km women, 10 km men, two shooting stages (prone, standing); misses mean 150 m loops.
Pursuit
Start gaps copied from the sprint results, 10 km women, 12.5 km men, four stages — the chase format.
Individual
15 km women, 20 km men, four stages; each miss adds one minute instead of a loop.

The season's top-ranked skiers together over 12.5 km women, 15 km men, with four shooting stages.
Relays
4x7.5 km per gender, plus mixed relay and single mixed relay — three spare rounds per stage, hand-loaded.
skills: Prone shooting
Flat on the ground, elbows anchored, sights steady on a 45 mm circle — the easier position with the smaller target.
Dry-fire ten minutes daily at home; live practice twice weekly with a coach checking position geometry.
Standing shooting
Offhand stance, knees soft, rifle locked high on the shoulder — 115 mm targets that look tiny at 170 beats per minute.
Train under load: twenty burpees, then five shots, repeated ten times — pulse control is the drill.
Range transitions
Arriving at race pace and leaving composed: ski in, breathe, five shots, ski out.
Rehearse full-speed entries every session, timing from the 200 m board to the first shot.
Pulse management
The last 200 meters before the range decide the shot — back off five percent and breathe in rhythm.
Interval sessions that end on the range; learn the personal pace that leaves your sight steady.
Skating under load
Racing with 3.5 kg on your back shifts balance and poling rhythm.
Do one rollerski session weekly with the rifle on; change nothing else.
Wind reading
Range flags and mirage tell how far to hold off center.
Deliberate wind sessions: aim upwind of the target and let the bullet drift — log every hold.
Zeroing
Sighting the rifle to the day's conditions before the start — a ritual, not a chore.
Confirm zeros after warmup with the coach; keep a logbook of zero notes per venue and weather.
rules: Each shooting stage is five targets; every miss costs a 150 m penalty loop, except individual races where a miss adds one minute.
Targets sit 50 m away: 45 mm diameter prone, 115 mm standing.
Rifles are .22 caliber, minimum 3.5 kg, carried on a harness — athletes never leave them at the range.
Skis, boots, and poles follow FIS cross-country rules; skating technique is universal.
Relays allow three spare rounds per stage, hand-loaded one at a time after the five-shot magazine fails.
Safety is absolute: shooting happens only from the assigned mat, and mishandling a rifle means disqualification.
equipment: Smallbore .22 with harness, diopter sights, and custom stock — $2,500-6,000 at race level.

Laser or air rifles for juniors and home dry-fire — $500-2,000.

Mats, spotting scopes, and a zeroing log — the club provides most of it.
training: The engine comes first: 500-700 hours a year of skiing, running, and rollerskiing, with weekly threshold and VO2max blocks.
Shooting is daily and small: dry-fire at home, limited perfect live rounds — sloppy volume builds sloppy habits.
Combined sessions are sacred: intervals that finish on the range train the sport's actual demand.
Strength for stability: anti-rotation core, upper back, and shoulder endurance hold the rifle still under fatigue.

name: Figure Skating
tagline: Quads on four-millimeter blades — a winter sport scored like gymnastics, danced like ballet.
overview: Figure skating is judged skating on one edge at a time: singles, pairs, and ice dance programs combine jumps, spins, steps, and lifts, scored since 2004 by the International Judging System — a technical score per element plus program component scores for artistry. The six jump types carry their inventors' names, and the Axel remains the only one taking off forward.

It is the oldest winter federation sport — the ISU dates to 1892 — and its cultural reach runs from Sonja Henie's Hollywood to national obsession in Japan, Canada, and across Europe. One clean quad can flip a championship; one fall can erase one, which is why the free skate is sport's most reliable four minutes of live tension.

Newcomers should know edges come before everything: crossovers, turns, and one-foot glides are the alphabet, jumps are sentences. Group lessons cost less than a dinner out, and progress is measured in seasons — the waltz jump to a single Axel is a two-year journey that teaches falling as a skill.
facts: ISU — International Skating Union, founded 1892, the oldest international winter sports federation
Men's and women's singles, pairs, ice dance, plus synchronized skating below the Olympics
International Judging System since 2004: technical element scores plus five program component scores
Six types — Axel, Lutz, flip, loop, Salchow, toe loop — with quadruple jumps now standard in men's events
Judged at the 1908 London Games and at every Winter Olympics since 1924
1896 in Saint Petersburg — the ISU's first world title of any kind
history: Jackson Haines fuses ballet and skating on tour in Europe; the international, dance-rooted style takes hold in Vienna.
The ISU is founded in the Netherlands and stages the first World Championships in Saint Petersburg in 1896.
Figure skating appears at the London Summer Olympics — the first judged winter sport in Olympic history, years before Winter Games existed.
Chamonix 1924 opens the Winter Games era; Sonja Henie wins three straight titles, and in 1961 the entire United States team dies in the Sabena crash en route to the Prague worlds.
Ice dance joins the Olympics at Innsbruck, completing the four-discipline program.
The Salt Lake City pairs scandal ends the 6.0 era; the International Judging System debuts in 2004 with per-element scoring.
formats: Singles
Short program of 2:40 with required elements, then a 4:00 free skate of open composition.
Pairs
Side-by-side jumps and spins plus overhead lifts, throw jumps, and twist lifts — strength choreographed.
Ice dance
Dance lifts and twizzles with no overt jumps; short dance plus free dance.
Synchronized skating
Sixteen skaters in formations — wheels, blocks, intersections — a world championship discipline since 2000.
Show skating
Touring shows and professional competitions keep retired champions on the ice — the sport's second stage.
skills: Edges
Deep, controlled one-foot leans — every jump, spin, and step grows from edge quality.
Power pulls and edge presses, fifteen minutes every session, both feet, both directions, no exceptions.
Jumps
Six types from waltz to quadruple: Axel takes off forward, Lutz from an outside edge, flip from inside — edge errors are called loudly.
Learn singles in order and land twenty consecutive clean singles before attempting doubles; harness work for new rotations.
Spins
Camel, sit, layback, and combination spins judged for speed, center, and positions.
Hold each position a minimum of eight rotations; enter from steps, not from standstill.
Twizzles
Multi-rotation traveling turns on one foot — ice dance's signature, done in unison.
Four sets of four twizzles down the rink daily; count aloud with your partner for sync.
Step sequences
Choreographed turns — brackets, counters, rockers, three-turns — linking end to end with rhythm.
Drill one turn family per week on figure circles; edge and turn vocabulary is memorized like scales.
Lifts
Overhead lifts in pairs and traveling lifts in dance — strength plus trust at height.
Progress only under a pairs coach with guarding; gym presses and carries build the base, never rushed on ice.
Performance
Program components score interpretation, musicality, and presence — expression is trainable.
Run full programs weekly under simulated judging; video every run-through and mark performance like you mark jumps.
rules: Competition runs a short program of 2:40 with required elements and a free skate of 4:00 with composition freedom.
The International Judging System scores each element: a base value plus a grade of execution from -5 to +5 by the judging panel.
Program components score skating skills, transitions, performance, composition, and interpretation of music — artistry is quantified, not guessed.
Under-rotated jumps are downgraded a full revolution's value, and a Lutz taken from the wrong inside edge — a flutz — is flagged by the technical panel.
Each fall carries a one-point deduction, and repeated jump types beyond the allowed count forfeit their value.
Costume, music, and time limits are policed — violations cost deductions rather than goodwill.
equipment: Stiff, heat-moldable boots fitted by a specialist — the sport's most personal purchase. $300-900.
Hollow-ground steel from makers like John Wilson and MK; competition pairs $200-600.
Blade guards for walking, absorbent soakers for storage — $15-30 that protect $500 blades.
Competition dresses and shirts range from $100 at club level to $1,500 bespoke.
The real cost of the sport: sessions run $10-30, and training skaters buy them by the season.
Off-ice rotation tools for daily practice at home. $50-200.
training: On-ice volume defines the sport: senior skaters train twenty or more hours weekly, split between elements and full run-throughs.
Off-ice jumps and spinner work daily; ballet or dance class weekly builds the carriage judges score under performance.
Strength is specific: single-leg power and rotational core for jumps, shoulder stability for lifts and spins.
Monitor jump load carefully — landings multiply body weight, and stress fractures are the sport's known cost.
Sport psychology is standard at the top: judged sports need routines for programs nobody can redo.
pathway: Learn-to-skate
Badge programs at any rink, any age — the universal front door.
Club testing
National test structures (moves in the field, freestyle, dance) grade progress beyond competitions.
Competitive sectional
Regional and sectional championships introduce the judged pipeline.
National and junior international
National championships and the Junior Grand Prix series.
Grand Prix, worlds, Olympics
The senior international circuit and its quadrennial summit.
events: Winter Olympics
Figure skating at every Winter Games since 1924, plus the team event since 2014.
World Championships
Annually since 1896 across singles, pairs, and dance.
Grand Prix series
Six autumn events — Skate America, Skate Canada and more — feeding a December final.
European and Four Continents Championships
The continental championships each January; Europe's dates to 1891.
Junior Grand Prix
The international development series for age-eligible juniors.
