United States — back-to-back Olympic titles (1948, 1952) and the first double Axel and triple loop landed in competition; the sport's great television voice.
Katarina Witt
Germany — consecutive Olympic titles in 1984 and 1988, capped by the Battle of the Carmens in Calgary.
Yuzuru Hanyu
Japan — back-to-back Olympic titles (2014, 2018), the first man to repeat in 66 years, and the first ratified quadruple loop.
Michelle Kwan
United States — five world titles and nine national titles; the standard of consistency and artistry for a decade.
getting_started: Start with group lessons at a rink's learn-to-skate program — rental skis first, fitted boots once you are hooked.
Insist on edges: every lesson should include crossovers, one-foot glides, and turns, not only jumping.
Add off-ice work early: hip and hamstring flexibility, core strength, and a spinner for rotation.
Protect the ankles: lace boots properly, check blade sharpness, and walk only with guards on.
Watch skating analytically — pick one element per viewing and count under-rotations like the technical panel does.
Budget patience: a clean single Axel is a milestone that routinely takes a year of consistent practice.
glossary: The only jump taking off from a forward edge — a half extra rotation that makes it the hardest.
A toe jump from an outside back edge, named for Alois Lutz.
A Lutz cheated from the wrong, inside edge — flagged by the technical panel.
An edge jump from a back inside edge, named for Ulrich Salchow.
A toe pick jump from a back outside edge, often used in combinations.
A fast multi-rotation traveling turn on one foot — ice dance's signature.
A spin position with the back arched and free leg turned out, classic in women's skating.
Grade of execution — the -5 to +5 mark judges add to each element's base value.
The five artistry scores: skating skills, transitions, performance, composition, interpretation.
The 2:40 required-element program that seeds the free skate.

name: Speed Skating (Long Track)
tagline: Racing the clock around a 400-meter oval — 60 km/h sprints to 25 grinding laps.
overview: Speed skating races the clock around a 400 m two-lane oval: pairs start together, change lanes each lap to equalize the corners, and the fastest time wins regardless of who they drew. Distances run from the 500 m sprint to the 10,000 m, plus team pursuit, team sprint, and the pack-style mass start.

It is the Netherlands in ice form — canal skating turned national religion — and recent decades have been Dutch by acclamation: at Sochi 2014 the Dutch won 23 of 36 speed skating medals. Eric Heiden's five golds at Lake Placid 1980 remain the sport's single greatest Olympic fortnight.

Newcomers should know the sport is technique first: a low position, sideways pushes, and patient crossovers beat fitness alone. Most Olympic ovals run public club nights with loaner skates, and the time-trial culture means personal bests arrive early and keep coming.
facts: ISU, founded 1892 — speed skating was one of its two founding sports
Standard 400 m oval, two lanes, with a lane change at each lap's back straight
500, 1000, 1500, 3000 (women), 5000, and 10,000 m, plus mass start and team events
Sprinters pass 60 km/h on the straights; the 10,000 m world record stands near 12:33
Men's races since Chamonix 1924; women's since Squaw Valley 1960
A hinged blade that extends the push, standard since the late 1990s and worth seconds per 1500 m
1889 in Amsterdam — the official world title predates the federation itself
history: Canal transport becomes national pastime in the Netherlands; iron skates and ice festivals turn commuting into racing.
Amsterdam stages the first official world championships over multiple distances.
The ISU is founded at Scheveningen to standardize distances, rules, and records.
Speed skating headlines the first Winter Olympics; women join the medal program at Squaw Valley 1960.
The clap skate escapes the laboratory and sweeps the World Cup within two seasons; world records fall across the board.
At Sochi the Netherlands wins 23 of 36 speed skating medals — depth no nation has approached before or since.
formats: Single distances
The Olympic core: one race, one medal, from 500 m sprints to the 10,000 m.
Sprint and allround championships
Two-day combined titles — sprinters race two 500s and two 1000s; allrounders race four distances under the Samalog point system.
Team pursuit
Three skaters ride formation for eight laps, six for women — the team time trial of ice.
Team sprint
Three skaters each lead one lap in sequence.
Mass start
Sixteen laps of pack racing with intermediate sprints — Olympic since 2018.
skills: The position
Hips low, back flat, hands behind — the racing stance is the sport's grammar and its gym.
Wall sits and isometric holds, three by 90 seconds daily; position endurance fails before legs do.
The push
Skating is pushing sideways from the hip through the full blade — not stepping.
Slide-board sessions twice weekly, three by ten minutes of slow, full-extension side pushes.
Crossunders
Fully crossing one leg over the other through every corner — free speed on the bends.
Twenty minutes of corner work every ice session; count crossovers per corner and never coast.
Starts
A running start into long, powerful strokes — the 500 m is decided in the first 100 m.
Twenty starts per session with first-100 m splits tracked weekly.
Aerodynamics
Hooded skinsuits, a flat back, and motionless hands — drag decides more than power at speed.
Film from the front to catch wobble; elites add wind-tunnel testing before big seasons.
Drafting in team racing
In pursuits and mass starts the lead skater breaks the wind — rotating well is a skill.
Practice formation changes with a partner every session: four laps leading, four laps following.
Pacing the 10,000
Twenty-five laps inside a half-second band per lap — the discipline of not panicking early.
Long threshold intervals, three by twelve minutes, with per-lap targets set in advance.
rules: Pairs race the clock, not each other — the fastest time across all pairs wins the distance.
Skaters change lanes every lap at the crossing in the back straight; interference there can bring a re-skate or disqualification.
False starts are charged to the pair; repeat offenders are disqualified.
In pairs there is no drafting and no pacing help — each duo races alone.
The mass start packs up to 24 skaters over 16 laps with three intermediate sprints worth points.
Timing runs to hundredths of a second, and a fall does not end a race — get up and finish the distance.
equipment: Clap-skate boots with hinged blades — $400-1,200 for a competitive setup.
Straight tube steel, sharpened by hand on a jig. $300-800.
The daily ritual — edges are checked before every session. $100-300.
Aero lenses for wind and ice spray. $40-150.
training: Aerobic volume is the base: 500-800 hours a year across cycling, running, and skating — the 10,000 m is an endurance race in tights.
Position strength: heavy squats and isometric holds in the racing position — the deep knee bend is the sport's gym signature.
Sprint work for the short distances: six to ten second maximum efforts and slide-board sprints build alactic power.
Hip mobility and adductor strength prevent the sport's classic overuse strains across the groin and hips.
Ice time is structured: technique drills first, intervals second — and every session ends with corners.
pathway: Learn-to-skate and club nights
Public sessions at ovals with loaner skates — most national champions started here.
Age-class racing
Regional meets and national junior championships, racing the clock from the start.
Junior internationals
World Junior Championships and development squads.
World Cup circuit
Five or six stops each winter across Europe, North America, and Asia.
World titles and Olympics
Single-distance, sprint, and allround championships, then the Games.
events: Winter Olympics
Speed skating's medal program since the first Winter Games in 1924.
ISU World Single Distances Championships
The annual distance-by-distance world title, since 1996.
World Allround and Sprint Championships
The classic combined titles decided over two days and four races each.
World Cup circuit
The winter league of paired racing at the sport's ovals, November to March.
Four Continents Championships
The ISU's championship for skaters outside Europe, first held in 2020.
legends: Eric Heiden
United States — five golds in five distances at Lake Placid 1980, the greatest single Games in speed skating history.
Ireen Wüst
Netherlands — six Olympic golds and 13 total medals, the most successful speed skater in Olympic history.
Sven Kramer
Netherlands — three consecutive 5000 m titles (2010, 2014, 2018) plus a team pursuit gold; the distance's defining racer.
Ard Schenk
Netherlands — three golds at Sapporo 1972 and the sport's first modern superstar.
Bonnie Blair
United States — five Olympic sprint golds across four Games from 1988 to 1994.
getting_started: Find the nearest 400 m oval's club night — most rent skates and coach beginners on the same evening.
Learn position and crossovers before chasing speed; a low back and bent knees are the whole sport's grammar.
Keep technique alive off-season with inline skating and a slide board.
Enter age-class meets early — long track's time-trial culture means personal bests are always available.
Take a sharpening lesson in week one; blade edges are a daily variable you will manage forever.
Choose a distance identity within a season — sprint and distance athletes train differently almost from the start.
glossary: The standard 400 m two-lane track, indoors or outdoors.
A hinged blade that stays on the ice longer, extending each push — universal since the late 1990s.
The full leg crossover through corners — free speed on the bends.
The marked change point in the back straight where skaters swap lanes each lap.
The points system converting times across distances into allround championships.
The combined format racing four distances over two days.
The two-skater starting unit in single-distance racing.
Pack racing over 16 laps with intermediate sprints, Olympic since 2018.
Three skaters in formation for eight laps, racing another team's trio.
The flat stretches between corners where the tuck lives.

name: Short Track Speed Skating
tagline: Six skaters, 111 meters of ice, medals decided in the last corner.
overview: Short track is pack racing on a 111.12 m oval marked inside a hockey rink: four to six skaters shoulder to shoulder over 500, 1000, and 1500 m, plus relays of 5000 m for men, 3000 m for women, and the mixed 2000 m. Placement decides everything — first across the line advances or wins — so tactics and nerve outrank raw lap times.

Born in North American racing carnivals and refined by Korea, China, and Canada, the sport has produced winter's most famous photo finishes and most famous crashes. Skaters lean so deep through corners that the left hand skims the ice — at 50 km/h, inches from four rivals.

Newcomers should know it is the most accessible elite skating: any hockey rink becomes a track with marker blocks. Learn to skate first, buy cut-resistant gloves immediately, and expect penalties to be part of the sport's grammar — impeding calls decide heats as often as legs do.
facts: A 111.12 m oval set with marker blocks on a standard rink — a kilometer is nine laps
Placement racing: the first skaters across the line advance or win; times seed heats only
Four to six skaters race each heat at once, shoulder to shoulder
Demonstration sport at Calgary 1988; full medals since Albertville 1992
ISU, with world championships since 1981 and a World Cup circuit since the 1990s
Hand-bent boots with blades around 45 cm, sharpened by hand on a jig
Cut-resistant suits, gloves, and helmets are mandatory — the blades are razor sharp
history: Early 1900s
Pack-style racing grows at North American skating carnivals on small rinks, long before Europe's ovals.
The ISU recognizes short track as a discipline.
International competition begins, and the first official ISU World Short Track Championships follow in 1981.
Demonstration status at Calgary, then full Olympic medals at Albertville 1992.
Yang Yang (A) wins China's first-ever Winter Olympic gold in the 500 m at Salt Lake City.
Viktor Ahn — the same Ahn Hyun-soo who starred for South Korea in 2006 — wins three golds and a bronze for Russia at Sochi.
formats: Four and a half laps of pure sprint — the first corner decides more than any other meter.
Nine laps, the tactical middle distance.
Thirteen and a half laps — pacing, patience, and a final three laps of chaos.
Relays
5000 m men (45 laps), 3000 m women (27 laps), and the mixed 2000 m, with push exchanges between teammates.
A championship super-distance raced for overall titles.
skills: Pack positioning
Where you sit in the line decides your race — sheltered, patient, with an exit.
Ride every position in training races; learn what third place can see that first cannot.
Inside passing
Slipping up the inside at corner entry — the sport's highest-risk, highest-reward move.
Inside-pass repetitions with a willing partner at 80 percent speed; commit late, stay low.
Outside passing
Swinging wide off a corner exit with more speed than the leader carried.
Outside-pass drills off every corner in warmups; time the swing against a coach's lap counter.
Corner technique
Deep lean, left hand brushing the ice, crossovers on every stride through the turn.
Twenty minutes of corner work every session — lean until the glove marks the ice, then repeat.
Starts
Explosive gun-to-first-corner acceleration — in the 500 m it is half the race.
Fifteen full-pack starts per session; solo starts teach nothing about the traffic you will meet.
Contact management
Shoulders will touch; balance under a bump is a skill, not luck.
Partner drills at 80 percent speed: jostle for lane legally, stay over your edges, no grabbing.
Push exchanges
The relay push that launches a teammate at full speed — timing beats power.
Twenty exchanges per relay practice; the push should arrive exactly at the corner exit.
rules: Racing is counterclockwise; the first skaters across the line advance or win, and times matter only for seeding.
Impeding — blocking, pulling, or forcing a rival off the racing line — draws penalties; the referee can advance an impeded skater instead.
Skaters must pass outside the marker blocks; cutting inside the blocks is a disqualification.
Helmets, cut-resistant suits, gloves, and shin protection are mandatory, and equipment is checked before racing.
Relays use push or touch exchanges, with the four skaters rotating through the race distance.
Advancement is generous by design: fastest losers and wronged skaters can advance on the referee's call.
equipment: Hand-bent boots with custom-mounted blades, sharpened on a jig — $800-2,500.
Around 45 cm, bent and offset for cornering — the sport's most personal tool. $300-700.
Cut-resistant suit and neck protection, mandatory. $300-800.
Cut-resistant, with hardened knuckle pads that skim the ice in corners. $50-150.
Worn under the suit against blade contact. $30-80.
training: Corner-specific dryland: low crossovers, wall sits, and slide-board work — corners are where races are held and lost.
Energy systems match the race: alactic sprints plus 45-second to two-minute anaerobic capacity intervals.
Ice sessions are pack sessions — four to five weekly, each with race-speed traffic; solo laps teach little.
Balance and contact: unstable-surface work and partner bumping drills make pressure survivable.
Weekly video review — call each pass before it happens, then check what actually happened.
pathway: Learn-to-skate
Basic skating confidence on any rink — hockey or recreational backgrounds both work.
Club pack racing
Local club nights set a 111 m track and teach positioning from the first session.
Provincial and national juniors
Age-class meets and junior championships from the early teens.
National team
Selection via national rankings; junior worlds usually arrive first.
World Cup and Olympics
The annual circuit across Asia, Europe, and North America, then the Games.
events: Winter Olympics
Short track's medal program since Albertville 1992.
ISU World Short Track Championships
The annual world title across individual distances and relays.
World Cup circuit
Several stops each winter — Seoul, Montreal, Dordrecht and more — with 500, 1000, and 1500 m races plus relays.
Four Continents Championships
The ISU championship for skaters outside Europe.
National championships
Deep domestic scenes in Korea, China, Canada, the Netherlands, and the United States.
legends: Apolo Anton Ohno
United States — eight Olympic medals including two golds across three Games; the face of American short track.
Viktor Ahn
South Korea and Russia — six medals for Korea in 2006, then three golds and a bronze for Russia at Sochi 2014; the most technically complete skater of the century.
Yang Yang (A)
China — the first Chinese Winter Olympic champion (500 m, Salt Lake City 2002) and a dominant early-2000s world force.
Suzanne Schulting
Netherlands — back-to-back Olympic 1000 m titles (2018, 2022) and consecutive overall world championship crowns.
Wu Dajing
China — Olympic 500 m champion at PyeongChang 2018 in 39.505 seconds, a world record that still stands.
getting_started: Any hockey rink works — clubs set the 111 m track with marker blocks on public nights.
Arrive with basic skating confidence; hockey, recreational, or long-track backgrounds all convert.
Buy cut-resistant gloves before anything else — most clubs will not let you on the ice without them.
Learn corner lean at low speed first: hand on the ice, weight inside, patience before pace.
Train in packs whenever possible — placement, not lap times, is the sport's actual skill.
Watch a full World Cup 1500 m on video and call the passes — the tactics live in the last two laps.
glossary: Racing shoulder to shoulder rather than against the clock.
A preliminary race; top finishers advance through rounds to the final.
Advance — the referee moving an impeded skater up despite the result.
Blocking or forcing a rival wide — the sport's cardinal penalty.
The rubber markers defining the track's corners.
Passing on the inside of a rival, usually at corner entry.
Swinging wide off a corner to pass with speed.
The relay handover where a teammate pushes the next skater into full speed.
The medal race of a distance, fed by semifinals and heats.
The camera-decided ending that short track produces more than any other skating discipline.

name: Bobsleigh
tagline: Half a ton of crew and sled at 150 km/h down an ice canyon.
overview: Bobsleigh crews sprint 50 m pushing a sled, dive aboard, and pilot 1,200-1,650 m of refrigerated ice track through 14-20 curves at up to 150 km/h, absorbing up to 5 G. Formats are two-man, four-man, two-woman, and the pilot-only monobob added at Beijing 2022 — and races are decided by hundredths across four heats.

The sport was invented for bored hotel guests at St. Moritz, where Caspar Badrutt built a run in the 1880s and the world's oldest bobsleigh club formed in 1897. Four-man bobsleigh headlined the first Winter Olympics in 1924, and Germany has since industrialized the sport into the deepest talent machine in winter racing.

Newcomers should know the two doors in: push athletes are recruited from sprinting with open national combines, while pilots attend federation driving schools that start with coach-driven descents. Most tracks also offer passenger rides — the cheapest way to understand why 5 G feels like a decision, not a sensation.
facts: IBSF — International Bobsleigh and Skeleton Federation, successor to the FIBT founded in 1923
Two-man, four-man, two-woman, and women's monobob
Maximums including crew: 630 kg four-man, 390 kg two-man, 330 kg two-woman — lighter crews add ballast
Refrigerated concrete, 1,200-1,650 m long, 14-20 curves, speeds to 150 km/h and corner forces near 5 G
Four-man since Chamonix 1924, two-man since 1932, women's since 2002, monobob since 2022
A 50 m sprint push in 4-6 seconds before loading — races are won here as often as in the curves
history: Caspar Badrutt builds a toboggan run for restless English guests at St. Moritz; the St. Moritz Bobsleigh Club forms in 1897 — the world's oldest.
The FIBT is founded in Paris, and four-man bobsleigh headlines the first Winter Olympics at Chamonix.
Two-man racing joins the program at Lake Placid.
Eugenio Monti lends rival Tony Nash an axle bolt at Innsbruck; Nash wins gold, and Monti collects the first Pierre de Coubertin medal for sportsmanship.
East Germany industrializes the sport — push tracks, sports science, talent pipelines — seeding today's German dynasty.
Women's racing debuts at Salt Lake City; monobob arrives at Beijing 2022 as Francesco Friedrich's era makes Germany the standard.
formats: Four-man
Pilot, brakeman, and two pushers — maximum crew at maximum speed.
Two-man
Pilot and brakeman; the purest test of a pilot's steering on long tracks.
Two-woman
The women's team discipline since 2002, sharing the same tracks and physics.
Monobob
One woman, one sled: push, load, steer, and brake alone — Olympic since 2022.
Championship format
Four heats over two days at the Olympics and worlds; World Cup races run two heats.
skills: Piloting
Steering by memorized line — entry points, apexes, and exit speeds for every named curve.
Federation driving schools: coach-steered descents first, then your hands on entry-level tracks, one curve at a time.
The push start
A 50 m all-out sprint pushing more than 200 kg of sled — the sport's most analyzed number.
Thirty-meter sprint work and loaded sled pushes three times weekly; crews time every push to the hundredth.
Loading
Diving aboard a moving sled without breaking rhythm — each crew has a choreographed entry.
Twenty load repetitions per session until the entry is silent and fast.
Braking
The brakeman alone pulls the brake after the finish line — a missed grab ends in the walls.
Brakemen double as pushers and train grip and reaction; the pull is rehearsed every descent.
G tolerance
Holding your head against 5 G for a minute while your vision narrows.
Daily isometric neck work — harness routines and holds; pilots and crew train it like a lift.
Steering precision
Two rope handles, subtle pulls, and a memory of twenty curves — oversteering costs speed, understeering costs walls.
Track walks and onboard video between every run; driving judgment is mileage, not talent.
Synchronization
A four-man push is four athletes with one stride pattern.
Weekly push-track sessions with video timing; the fastest crews sync strides to the sled frame.
rules: The run begins with the sprint push; timing starts as the sled crosses the start gate and stops at the finish.
Maximum weights include crew and equipment: 630 kg four-man, 390 kg two-man, 330 kg two-woman — lighter crews may add ballast, heavier crews are disqualified.
Runners are standardized steel within strict IBSF dimensions — no custom machining and no heating between runs.
Olympic and world titles are decided by the lowest aggregate time over four heats; the sled must finish with its full crew aboard.
The brakeman operates the brake only after the finish line; steering is the pilot's alone, via two handles linked to the front axle.
Suits, helmets, and shoes are regulated — push shoes carry brush spikes that grip the start ice.
equipment: IBSF-spec carbon and steel machines; new race sleds run $30,000-90,000.
Polished steel, ground to spec per track — a set costs $1,500-4,000.
Sprint shoes with brush spikes for start traction. $100-300.
Aerodynamic skinsuits regulated like speed skating's. $200-500.
Not sold but essential — summer wheeled tracks are where crews are built.
training: Push athletes are sprinters: 30-60 m acceleration, heavy squats, and power cleans are the core program.
Neck strength is daily: isometric holds and harness work for corners that hit 5 G.
Pilots accumulate descents year-round — summer ice at Calgary and push tracks keep driving judgment alive.
Track walks and video study are training: most tracks are learned by name, curve by curve.
Injury prevention: Nordic curls and hamstring work for sprint loads, shoulder stability for pushing.
pathway: Open combines
National federations test 30 m sprints, jumps, and squats — the recruitment door for push athletes.
Development team
Push-track training, brakeman duty, and passenger runs behind experienced pilots.
Driving school
Federation schools on real ice for aspiring pilots — braking runs before steering.
Continental Cups
The North American and European circuits where new crews and pilots earn ranks.
World Cup and Olympics
The sport's summit, dominated in the modern era by Germany's system.
events: Winter Olympics
On the program since the first Winter Games in 1924.
IBSF World Championships
Annual except Olympic years, shared with skeleton.
World Cup circuit
Stops at St. Moritz, Altenberg, La Plagne, Lake Placid, Whistler and more each winter.
Continental Cups
The North American and European development circuits.
Continental championships
The European and North American titles feeding world rankings.
legends: Eugenio Monti
Italy — six Olympic medals in the 1950s and 1960s, and the 1964 Pierre de Coubertin medal for lending a rival the bolt that won gold.
Wolfgang Hoppe
Germany — double Olympic champion at Sarajevo 1984 and a medalist across a decade of East German dominance.
Kevin Kuske
Germany — four Olympic golds as brakeman beside André Lange and Francesco Friedrich; the sport's greatest pusher.
Francesco Friedrich
Germany — Olympic champion in both disciplines at Beijing 2022 and the most decorated pilot in history.
Kaillie Humphries
Canada and the United States — two-woman titles in 2010 and 2014 for Canada, the first monobob gold in 2022 for the United States.
getting_started: Test as a push athlete first: national combines measure 30 m sprints, broad jumps, and squats — those numbers get you recruited.
Ride before you drive: every driving school starts with coach-driven and braking runs on real ice.
Use summer push tracks with wheeled sleds to build the sprint-load skill year-round.
Pick your door honestly — brakemen are fast-twitch athletes; pilots are students of geometry with ten years of patience.
Watch onboard footage of Altenberg or St. Moritz and name the curves — memorization is the pilot's first training.
Build the three currencies: sprint speed, squat strength, and neck endurance.
glossary: The athlete who steers, via two handles linked to the front axle.
The rear crew member who pulls the brake after the finish line.
The side crew members in four-man who load mid-sled.
The dive aboard at speed — choreographed, rehearsed, and make-or-break.

name: Skeleton
tagline: Head first at 130 km/h, steering with shoulders and knees — no brakes.
overview: Skeleton races a small sled head first and prone: athletes sprint 25-40 m bent over their sled, dive aboard, and ride 1,200-1,650 m of ice track at up to 140 km/h with corner forces near 5 G. There is no brake and no steering mechanism — the body does the driving.

The sport grew out of the Cresta Run, built at St. Moritz for the winter of 1884-85, and it is winter sliding's most accessible elite door: national slide schools take complete beginners onto real ice in days, and adult sprinters regularly reach national teams within a few seasons.

Newcomers should know the order of operations: the push decides the run, the load decides the push, and the line decides everything else. Fear is managed, not eliminated — every national team member started on a beginner track with a coach walking them through curve one.
facts: IBSF — skeleton races under the bobsleigh federation's roof
Prone and head first, face centimeters above the ice
120-145 km/h with corner forces approaching 5 G; the sled has no brakes
Shoulder, knee, and head pressure — no mechanical steering exists
St. Moritz 1928 and 1948, then a 54-year absence until Salt Lake City 2002
Combined athlete-plus-sled maximums of 115 kg (men) and 102 kg (women), with ballast allowed for lighter athletes

skills: The push
A bent-over sprint with the sled, 25-40 m, worth a tenth or more at the finish.
Thirty-meter sprint work plus push-track sessions two or three times weekly, timed on video.
The load (dive)
Belly-down onto a moving sled at 30 km/h — the make-or-break skill of the sport.
Dive mechanics drilled at walking speed first, then half pace; twenty loads per session, speed added gradually.
Line reading
The shortest line through 14-20 named curves at 130 km/h — memorized, not seen.
Track walks and onboard video before every first run; rehearse the line mentally between heats.
Head discipline
Chin up a centimeter too far scrapes the visor and costs the run — the neck holds position under 5 G.
Isometric neck training three times weekly — harness routines and holds.
Steering
Shoulder and knee pressure, tiny and early — the sled has no other controls.
Beginner-track progressions at Lillehammer or Calgary: straight runs, then gentle curves, then full lines.
Fear management
Composure at 130 km/h face down is trainable: routines, breathing, and exposure in careful doses.
Process routines before every run; progression through tracks rather than heroic leaps.
Sled preparation
Polishing steels is a nightly ritual; runner condition is worth hundredths nobody sees.
Learn runner polishing and sled assembly first — mechanics is the entry-level skill every slider needs.
rules: The clock starts at the start beam; every hundredth lost in the push shows up at the finish.
Combined athlete-plus-sled weight is capped — about 115 kg men, 102 kg women — and lighter athletes add ballast to reach it.
Sleds are frame-and-runner machines within IBSF size specs; no brakes and no mechanical steering are permitted.
A run is invalid if the athlete comes off the sled — riders stay aboard from start to finish.
Full-face helmets with chin guards, speed suits, and spiked shoes are mandatory equipment.
Olympic races run four heats over two days with the lowest aggregate time winning.

Isometric neck work starts in week one — the first fast corner explains why immediately.
Track walks and onboard video are daily training during race weeks; skeleton is a memory sport.
Posterior-chain strength — Romanian deadlifts, hip thrusts — and anti-rotation core serve the load position.
Confidence is built by progression: beginner tracks, longer tracks, then the classic tracks — never skipped rungs.

name: Luge
tagline: Feet first at 140 km/h — decided by thousandths of a second, not by brakes.
overview: Luge races a small sled feet first and supine down refrigerated tracks at up to 140 km/h: athletes pull start handles, paddle the ice for acceleration, then steer with calf pressure on the runners and subtle shoulder shifts. There are no brakes and no second chances — timing is measured to the thousandth of a second, the finest margin in winter sport.

Germany, Austria, and Italy have owned the podium since luge joined the Olympics at Innsbruck 1964, and the sport's culture is intimate: small national teams, family sled workshops, and classic tracks where generations learn the same curves. Team relay added a crowd format in 2014; women's doubles joins the Olympic program at Milano Cortina 2026.

Newcomers should know the start is half the sport — paddle power and coordination decide an outsized share of the result. National federation start schools teach the sequence on real ice with loaner sleds, and natural-track luge offers an accessible alpine variant for clubs without a concrete channel.

Calf pressure against the runners and shoulder shifts — no brakes anywhere on the sled

skills: The start
Rock the sled, pull the handles, and paddle the ice explosively before lying onto the pod — the sport's most-trained sequence.
Start-track sessions weekly; paddle power built with bench pulls, rows, and medicine-ball slams.
Calf steering
Pressing a calf against the runner flexes the steel and steers that side — the sport's core control skill.
Single-curve focus runs: ten passes working only one corner, hands quiet, legs doing the talking.
Shoulder and body control
Shoulder rolls and weight shifts fine-tune the line where calves cannot.
Onboard video after every run; compare pressure points curve by curve with a coach.
Head discipline
Lying flat, chin down, racing from memory — visibility is sacrificed to aerodynamics.
Memorization drills: track walks, curve names, and sector splits recited before every run.
Line precision
Enter high, clip the apex, exit low — identical every time.
Sector-timed runs; the goal is not one fast line but ten identical ones.
Doubles teamwork
Two on one sled: the front athlete steers, the back athlete adds weight and balance.
Partner starts and sync drills; doubles teams are chosen for complementary sizes and trust.
Relay handovers
The touchpad relay demands three clean runs, back to back, from one squad.
Full relay rehearsals in training camps; pad timing teaches urgency better than any stopwatch.

Sleds are FIL-spec machines with maximum weights around 21-25 kg for singles and 25-30 kg for doubles.
Runner temperature is checked at the start — warming steels for speed is against the rules.
Olympic men's singles run four heats and women's singles two since 2022; the lowest combined time wins.
The team relay chains men's single, women's single, and doubles runs; the next sled launches the instant the previous one trips the touchpad.
A run ends if the athlete comes off the sled — no re-boarding, no second chances.

Track memory is daily training: video, curve names, and sector splits rehearsed like a script.

Hollow-body isometrics mirror the race position — the flat, tensioned profile that wins straightaways.

name: Curling
tagline: Nineteen-kilogram granite stones, brooms, and eight ends of geometry on ice.
overview: Curling is precision team play on ice: teams of four slide 19-kg granite stones down a 45.72 m sheet toward the house, a target of four concentric rings, while teammates sweep to adjust speed and curve. Only one team scores per end — the team with the stones closest to the button — and the last-stone advantage, the hammer, shapes every strategic choice.

Scotland wrote the rules and Canada wrote the culture: club curling is a civic institution across the northern latitudes, bonspiels run from village leagues to the Scotties and the Brier, and the sport's Olympic revival since 1998 turned skips into household names. It is often called chess on ice, and the comparison holds — visible strategy, invisible margins.

Newcomers should find a learn-to-curl session: two hours, all gear included, and you will throw takeouts in week one. The delivery is a lunge, balance is the whole game, and honesty is built in — players call their own fouls, which tells you what kind of sport this is.
facts: World Curling Federation, the international federation since 1966
Four players — lead, second, vice-skip, and skip — each throwing two stones per end
45.72 m (150 ft) long and about 5 m wide, pebbled with water droplets that make stones curl
Concentric rings of 12, 8, and 4 feet around the button at the center
17.24-19.96 kg granite from Ailsa Craig, Scotland — shaped and polished by Kays of Scotland
Medal event at Chamonix 1924, recognized retroactively in 2006, and continuously since Nagano 1998
Ten ends in championship play; eight ends in club games and mixed doubles
history: The first written record of curling appears in Scotland — a game on frozen ponds already old when written down.
Kilsyth's curling club traces itself to 1716, the sport's oldest traced club.
The Grand Caledonian Curling Club standardizes the laws of the game; royal patronage in 1843 adds the Royal to its name.
Curling is played at the first Winter Olympics in Chamonix; the IOC confirms its medal status in 2006.
Curling returns as a full medal sport at Nagano — television discovers the sweep.
Mixed doubles debuts at PyeongChang 2018, and the four-player mixed team event joins at Beijing 2022.
formats: Team curling
The classic four-player game, ten ends at championships — strategy at its deepest.
Mixed doubles
Two players, eight ends, each team throwing five stones with one pre-positioned — fast, tactical, Olympic since 2018.
Mixed team
Two men and two women alternating — an Olympic event since Beijing 2022.

skills: Delivery
A balanced lunge from the hack: stone on line, slide low, release smooth.
A hundred dry slides a week — balance beats power; a knee-slide drill on the back line teaches the weight transfer.
Draw weight
Throwing a stone to stop on the button without sweeping — the calibrated memory at the heart of the game.
Time every throw with a stopwatch and log it; ten draws per practice to a target, in-turn and out-turn.
Takeouts
Removing opponent stones with weight and angle — peel weight clears guards at maximum pace.
Set target stones and throw ten takeouts per practice; hit-and-rolls teach angle control.
Sweeping
Friction control in real time: sweeping adds distance, straightens the path, and is the difference between a point and a blank.
Forty-five-second maximum-effort sweep intervals — the position is an aerobic sport in disguise.
Reading the ice
Every sheet curls differently by the minute — frost, humidity, and pebble all shift the line.
Throw a dozen draws at the start of every session and chart where they stopped.
Calling (skipping)
The skip reads the end, chooses shots, and shows the broom — decision-making under a running clock.
Score your own decisions like statisticians do; replay one end after every game and defend the calls aloud with your team.
Handle (rotation)
In-turn and out-turn rotations decide whether the stone curls in or out — the same weight, two personalities.
Alternate rotations throw by throw; mirror drills with the non-dominant hand build feel.
rules: Ten ends in championship play, eight in most club games: each team throws eight stones per end, two per player.
Only one team scores per end — one point for each of its stones closer to the button than the opponent's best.
The scoring team throws first the following end, surrendering the hammer; the team with hammer throws last, the key advantage.
The five-rock rule protects guards: stones in the free guard zone cannot be removed from play before the fifth stone of the end, a WCF standard since 2018.
Deliveries must be released before the near hog line, and stones must cross the far hog line to stay in play.
Touching a moving stone is a foul — the non-offending team chooses the remedy — and players call their own violations.
equipment: Ailsa Craig granite at $400-700 each — clubs own them; players never do.
Carbon-fiber shaft with a WCF-certified pad head. $100-300.
One slider sole (PTFE), one gripper — or a slip-on slider over a sneaker to start. $100-250.
Pushes the stone from a standing position — the stick curling tool and an accessibility lifeline. $40-80.
Timed deliveries are how draw weight is learned. $10-30.
Flexible pants and layers you can lunge in — ice arenas sit near freezing.
training: Sweeping fitness is the hidden athletic base: interval training that mimics 45-second maximum efforts.
Balance work — single-leg squats, lunges, and stability drills — carries directly into delivery consistency.
Throw volume with intent: every practice includes timed draws to a target and charted results.
Strategy study: watch Grand Slam matches with the skip's decisions in mind and pause before each call.
Hip and ankle mobility keep the delivery lunge deep and repeatable across a season of league nights.
